evidence.label: The Falconer distance conjecture in all dimensions

headline: Any set bigger than half the dimension of its space has distances that fill a stretch of positive length.
scope: The result covers compact sets in every dimension d of 2 or more. Their dimension must be strictly above d/2.
plain: Take a set of points and list every distance between two of them. Falconer asked how large the set must be before those distances cover a stretch of real length. The expected answer was a dimension above half that of the space. This paper proves that answer in every dimension (Lean proof listed). It needs no assumption about how regular the set is.
doesNot: This does not cover sets of dimension exactly d/2, or distances measured from one single point.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles a conjecture open since 1985 in every dimension. Earlier work stopped at partial thresholds.

visual.title: Best general dimension threshold in the plane
visual.note: Smaller is better. 1 is the conjectured value; the threshold itself is not covered.

explanation:
Draw a square and cut it into a 4 by 4 grid of 16 small squares. Keep 5 of them and throw the rest away. Now repeat the same step inside each square you kept, forever. After 5 steps you hold 3125 tiny squares, each 1/1024 of the side. Together they cover about 0.3 percent of the original area. In the limit the area is zero. What remains is a fractal dust of points.

Now measure every distance between two points of that dust. The distances all lie between 0 and about 1.414, the diagonal. The question is whether they cover a stretch of that range with real length. A finite set of points gives only finitely many distances, so the length is zero. A full square gives every distance from 0 to 1.414. The dust sits in between.

The right yardstick is Hausdorff dimension. It is a way to give a set a size between whole numbers. A line has dimension 1 and a filled square has dimension 2. Our dust multiplies its pieces by 5 while shrinking them by 4 at each step. That gives it dimension log 5 / log 4, about 1.16. The plane has dimension 2, so half of that is 1. The dust is above that halfway mark.

In 1985, K. J. Falconer asked what dimension forces the distances to have positive length. Positive length here means positive Lebesgue measure, the usual notion of total length on a line. He showed that dimension above (d+1)/2 is enough, where d is the dimension of the space. In the plane that is 1.5. He also gave lattice-type examples at exactly d/2. These explain why the conjecture asks for dimension strictly greater than d/2.

Later work pushed the planar threshold down. Thomas Wolff reached 4/3 in 1999. Guth, Iosevich, Ou and Wang reached 5/4 in 2020, with distances measured from a single point. Our dust, at about 1.16, sits below all of these. In three dimensions, Du, Ou, Ren and Zhang reached about 1.714 in a 2024 preprint. The target there is 1.5. Recent work reached the halfway mark only for unusually regular sets. Liu's planar result, for example, needed two different measures of dimension to agree.

This paper proves the full conjecture in every dimension d of 2 or more. Take any compact set, meaning closed and bounded, in d-dimensional space. If its Hausdorff dimension is above d/2, its distances have positive length. In the plane, any such set above dimension 1 qualifies, including the dust. The theorem asks for no regularity at all. A set may be as patchy and uneven as it likes.

The main obstacle shows up in higher dimensions. Stand at one point of the set and look at the other points. Note the direction to each one. Those directions form a set on a sphere. For a set of dimension just above d/2, they can be too thin to spread out evenly. So earlier tools that assume an even spread cannot start. The paper instead builds a weaker guarantee: no small patch of directions holds too much of the set. It then shows that this weaker guarantee is enough for the distance estimate.

The result has clear edges. It says nothing at dimension exactly d/2. It is about all distances between pairs of points. It does not claim that the distances measured from one single point have positive length. It also gives positive length, which is stronger than saying the distances have dimension 1.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked a formal version of the main theorem. It covers every dimension d of 2 or more. A separate Lean statement covers the planar case. Specialists have not published a review yet.
hypeCheck: Landmark if the proof holds. Lean has checked formal statements of the main theorem and the planar case. No specialist review has been published, and the endpoint d/2 and the single-point version stay open.
